column4: “Worship Me” (وَأَنِ ٱعْبُدُونِى) is itself “a straight path”; it makes the section’s meeting of willing servitude and the requested road an explicit Qur’anic identity.
Jesus calls God “my Lord and your Lord,” then says “worship Him; this is a straight path”; the true Rabb, direct address, worship, and road remain one claim.
Jesus again joins the shared Lordship of God to “worship Him” and “a straight path,” confirming that the section’s road is a relation to its real owner.
Jesus’ command to worship the one Lord concludes “this is a straight path”; it gives the section’s servant-and-road image another exact formulation.
“Upon God is the direction of the way,” while some ways are crooked (جَائِرٌ); this is the section’s herdsman-guide scene stated as a divine distinction between a straight route and deviation.
The livestock’s beauty appears when they return at evening and go out to pasture; it is the herd’s outward journey and return immediately before the path of 16:9.
The animals carry people’s burdens to a land they could reach only with hardship; it gives the section’s weary traveller and animal-road image its concrete travel burden.
God creates livestock for warmth, benefits, and food; this grounds the section’s herd in provision from the Rabb rather than in an ownerless animal.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are made for riding and adornment; this extends the passage’s movement along a road through animals fitted to carry people.
Rain becomes drink and vegetation in which livestock pasture; it joins the section’s water, plant, herd, and sustaining-Rabb images in the same sequence as the road passage.

The earth is made ذَلُولًا for people to walk its shoulders and seek provision. The section’s dictionary adjective “müzellel” therefore makes tractable ground, walking, and dependence on provision meet.
The cow is described as not ذَلُولٌ, not broken to plough earth or water crops. This negative boundary sharpens the section’s “müzellel” animal/path sense and its link to earth and water.
God creates livestock and makes humans their owners; it supplies the ownership side of the section’s contrast between a known Rabb and the ownerless, stray animal.
“We subdued them for them” (وَذَلَّلْنَٰهَا) makes some livestock mounts and some food; the section’s tamed animal and service relation is directly enacted.
Livestock provide benefits and drink; the verse completes the preceding subjugation with the provision for which the dependent servant gives praise.
Pilgrims come walking and on lean camels from every distant pass. It gives the section’s road a bodily journey whose destination is the House.
At the pilgrimage people mention God’s name over the livestock He provided, then eat and feed the needy; herd, divine name, provision, and purposeful arrival coincide.
The sacrificial animals have benefits until an appointed term, then their place is at the Ancient House; it is the section’s animal carried onward to its home.
Each community is given a rite to mention God’s name over provided livestock, followed by “submit to Him.” This makes sacrifice a voluntary servitude to the one God.
The camels are God’s symbols: His name is spoken over them, they fall, and people eat and feed others. It supplies the fully staged sacrificial-herd scene behind the section’s meeting.
God subdues the animals so people may magnify Him “for what He guided you to” (عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَىٰكُمْ). It explicitly joins tamed herd, praise, and guidance on the way.
The command names sacrificial animals, their garlands, and those heading for the Sacred House seeking bounty and pleasure. It joins the guide/offering word-field to a directed journey home.
An expiation can be livestock “as an offering reaching the Kaʿbah” (هَدْيًا بَٰلِغَ ٱلْكَعْبَةِ); it gives the section’s home-bound sacrifice its exact arrival.
The Kaʿbah, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands are made a قيامًا for people. The House, herd, and the section’s image of standing are gathered in one verse.
The opponents hold back the sacrificial offering from reaching its place. This is the concrete reverse of the section’s animal being taken safely to the House.
The first House set for people at Bakkah is blessed and “guidance for the worlds.” It gives the section’s road an endpoint that is both a house and guidance.
The House contains clear signs and pilgrimage is due from whoever can find a way to it. The verse makes finding the road to the House a duty before the true owner.
The House is made a place of return and safety, with Abraham’s standing-place made a prayer place. It realizes the section’s return-home and upright-worship imagery.
“My prayer and my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds.” Sacrifice is here explicitly owned by the Rabb rather than by a merely human keeper.
Pharaoh says, “Did we not raise you among us as a child?” (نُرَبِّكَ). The source section’s raising word becomes a coercive claim of false nurture.
Pharaoh follows his claimed upbringing by indicting Moses for his deed and calling him among the ungrateful. Its accusation exposes the pressure beneath the supposed favor of 26:18.
Moses says he acted while among the ضَالِّينَ. In the same exchange, lostness answers Pharaoh’s claimed raising and anticipates the section’s road imagery.
After fleeing in fear, Moses says “my Lord gave me judgment and made me one of the messengers.” The real Rabb gives vocation where Pharaoh claimed a debt.
Moses calls Pharaoh’s alleged favor the fact that he enslaved the Children of Israel. It is the section’s decisive reversal: imposed bondage masquerading as nurture versus chosen worship.
Moses defines the real Lord to Pharaoh as the one who gives every thing its creation and then guides it. It fuses true Rabbhood, fitting a creature, and leading it onward.
The prayer asks mercy for parents “as they raised me small” (رَبَّيَانِى). It gives non-coercive human nurture the merciful counterpart to Pharaoh’s boast.
Pregnancy, weaning, reaching full strength, and gratitude for God’s favor occur in one life arc. It makes the section’s womb, maturation limit, and completed blessing concrete.
Mothers nurse for two complete years “for whoever wishes to complete nursing.” The verse supplies the section’s precise boundary at which nurture reaches completion.
God forms people in their mothers’ wombs, creation after creation, then calls Himself their Rabb whose is all dominion. Womb, nurturing Lord, and ownership coincide.
God forms people in wombs as He wills. It gives the section’s formative mercy an explicit divine act rather than an impersonal growth.
What God wills remains in wombs to an appointed term, then emerges a child and reaches full strength. It maps the section’s growth toward its measured completion.
The embryo’s successive formations culminate in “another creation.” This makes the section’s shaped-in-the-womb image a sequence of deliberate making.
Jacob says the Lord will complete His favor on Joseph and Jacob’s family as before. It supplies the section’s completed نعمة as an act of the knowing Rabb.
God announces that He has perfected religion, completed His favor, and approved submission. The section’s completed blessing reaches its communal and worshipful form here.
After purification for prayer, God says He intends to complete His favor so people may give thanks. It links finished favor to the worshipper’s bodily approach.
God’s direction of faces is “so that I may complete My favor upon you and so that you may be guided.” Completion and way-finding are explicitly paired.
Completing the counted days is followed by magnifying God for having guided you. It echoes the section’s 22:37 meeting of completion, praise, and guidance.
After naming shelters, shade, and protective provision, God says He completes His favor so people may submit. It joins nurture, shelter, completion, and willing servitude.
God found the Prophet an orphan and gave shelter; this supplies a non-Pharaonic image of the Rabb’s unclaimed, protective nurture.
“Found you ضَالًّا and guided” places lostness and guidance inside that same merciful care, like the section’s stray animal found by its true guide.
“Found you in need and made you self-sufficient” completes the trio with provision, clarifying what true divine upbringing gives without reproach.
Moses is told to remind his people of “the days of God,” signs for the patient and grateful. It gives the section’s days a history of punishment and favor, not a neutral calendar.
Believers are told to forgive those who do not await God’s days, when He will repay each people for what they earned. It makes those days days of moral reckoning.
Following God’s pleasure is set against returning with His anger and Hell. It gives the section’s rıza/gazap division a direct final-destination contrast.
God guides those who seek His pleasure to ways of peace and brings them from darkness to light. Divine pleasure becomes a route, answering the section’s angry fall from the way.
Those cursed and angered by God are described as farther astray from the sound way. It directly binds غضب, straying, and the section’s two endings of the road.
God warns that whoever His anger settles upon “has fallen” (فَقَدْ هَوَىٰ). The section’s anger descending and the traveller’s fall are the verse’s own physical verdict.
After repentance, faith, and good work, God says He forgives and then guides. It supplies the risen, reoriented counterpart to the fall under anger in 20:81.
The comparison is between one walking fallen on his face and one walking upright on a straight road. It is the section’s fall-versus-upright-guidance image stated bodily.
“Faces that day will be naʿimah” (نَاعِمَةٌ), soft or blissful. It is the section’s named face on the favorable side of the Day.
“Faces that day” bear dust (عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌ). It provides the section’s opposing, dust-covered face of judgment.
Radiant faces on that Day supply another visible form of favor, strengthening the section’s claim that the Day appears on faces.
Gloomy, frowning faces expect a crushing calamity. Their expression supplies the adverse boundary to the Day’s radiant faces.
The radiance of bliss is recognizable in their faces. This turns the section’s “mark” and favorable Day-face into a visible sign of final provision.

The debt verse fixes term, writing, witnesses, the possibility that one may “go astray/forget” (تَضِلَّ), and testimony that is more upright (أَقْوَمُ). It concretizes debt, lostness, and standing straight.
The immediately preceding warning says every soul will return to God and be paid in full for what it earned. It gives the contract’s careful accounting its final Day horizon.
God raises the sky and sets the balance. It gives the section’s noon-scale image its Qur’anic meeting of height and measured equilibrium.
The command not to transgress the balance establishes a boundary between an upright measure and its bending or excess.
“Establish weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient” makes upright weighing the ethical counterpart to the section’s standing scale.
“Woe to the defrauders” introduces the scene in which a tilted measure becomes a matter for the Lord of all worlds.
Those who take full measure from people enact the receiving side of the section’s balance-and-debt image.
When they measure or weigh for others, they cause loss. This is the precise reversal of the level scale the section invokes.
The defrauders are asked whether they think they will be raised; their practical fraud is turned toward the standing of the Day.
“That tremendous Day” names the horizon that turns ordinary weighing into final accountability.
People will stand (يَقُومُ) before the Lord of the worlds. It directly joins the section’s qiyām image, balance, and the Rabb of 1:2.
Just balances are set up for the Day of Resurrection, with even a mustard seed brought forth. The verse makes the section’s scale explicitly a final accounting device.
The weighing on that Day is truth, and heavy scales bring success. It gives the section’s level balance its decisive outcome.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves because they wronged the signs. It supplies the opposite fate of the upright measure.
One whose scales are heavy receives a pleasing life; this makes weight on the Day a lived result rather than an abstraction.
One whose scales are light has the abyss as mother. It adds the catastrophic reverse of the section’s balanced standing.
Book and balance are sent down “so that people may stand for justice” (لِيَقُومَ ٱلنَّاسُ بِٱلْقِسْطِ). It explicitly ties measure to standing upright.
The question “What will make you know the Day of Recompense?” makes dīn the Day’s active reckoning, clarifying the section’s debt-day sense.
On that Day no soul controls anything for another, and command belongs wholly to God. It supplies the section’s kingly ownership at the close of debt.
On the Day people are exposed, God asks whose is sovereignty today and answers: the One, the Overpowering. It makes the Day’s Malikship audible.
Leaving toward Midian, Moses asks his Lord to guide him to the level way (سَوَاءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ). It gives the section’s water-and-road scene its initial request for direction.
At Midian’s water Moses finds a group watering and two women holding back their flock. It supplies the missing well and herd scene between road and shade.
After watering for them, Moses withdraws to shade and confesses need for whatever good his Lord sends. Water, shade, service, and dependence meet in one prayer.
One of the women comes to invite Moses to her father, giving the well episode a human destination after his road, water, and shaded plea.
God makes earth a cradle, makes paths through it, and sends water from the sky to bring out pairs of plants. It directly unites road, water, and sustaining formation.
“Eat and pasture your livestock” follows the road-and-water verse. It gives the section’s herd its share in the same divine provision.
If they had remained upright on the way, God would have given them abundant water. The conditional makes straightness and water meet with unusual exactness.
Winds carry heavy clouds, rain is sent to dead land, and fruits emerge. The section’s cloud-and-plant nurture is staged as renewal from God.
Good land yields vegetation by its Lord’s permission while bad land yields only scant growth. It gives nourishment a moral and relational contrast without changing the scene.
By rain God grows crops, olives, dates, grapes, and all fruits. It extends the nearby pasture-water scene into the plant nourishment named in the section.
God brings forth earth’s water and pasture. This concise pairing supplies the section’s linked provision for traveller and herd.
The water and pasture are provision for people and their livestock, making the prior cosmic preparation explicitly shared sustenance.
Abraham calls God the one who created him and then guides him. It begins the section’s ordered confession with formation becoming a personal route.
Abraham says God feeds him and gives him drink. It supplies the water and nourishment step after guidance.
Abraham adds that when he is ill, God heals him. Its bodily need continues the same speech of dependence between drinking and death.
God causes Abraham to die and will bring him to life. This is the passage’s bridge from daily provision toward its Day-of-recompense ending.
Abraham hopes that God will forgive him on the Day of Recompense. It supplies the section’s final dīn-day step in the same first-person sequence.
Abraham sees a rising star, calls it “my Lord,” then rejects it when it sets. It begins the section’s test of a rising sign against the true Rabb.
With the moon, Abraham says that unless his Lord guides him he will be among the ضَالِّينَ. Celestial appearance, true guidance, and lostness meet explicitly.
The rising sun is called larger, then rejected at its setting; Abraham disavows association. It completes the section’s sequence of elevated but non-divine signs.
Abraham turns his face to the Originator of heavens and earth as a hanīf, not an associator. It names the true referent behind the signs.
God shows Abraham the dominion of heavens and earth before the star, moon, and sun scene. It frames those objects as signs within divine dominion.
In disputing over his Lord, Abraham answers a false sovereign with God’s bringing the sun from the east; the ruler is confounded and not guided. Sovereignty, rising sun, and guidance converge.
A people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Satan beautifies this and bars them from the way, so they are not guided. It is the section’s exact failure to distinguish sign from its Lord.
The following call is to prostrate to God, who brings out what is hidden in heavens and earth. It states the corrective object of worship to 27:24’s sun worship.
Night, day, sun, and moon are signs; people are forbidden to prostrate to sun or moon and commanded to prostrate to their Creator. This directly explains the section’s sign/referent distinction.
“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High” joins the section’s opening name to elevation and praise before the Rabb.
“Read in the name of your Lord who created” makes a named Rabb the source of creation, matching the section’s beginning with a name and its formative Lord.
God may be called Allah or the Merciful, for His are the most beautiful names. It lets the section’s opening name hold both divine identity and the Rahman/Rahim relation.
“God’s dye/mark” (صِبْغَةَ ٱللَّهِ) is followed by “we are worshippers of Him.” It gives the section’s brand image a mark that identifies voluntary worship rather than an idol.
The worshippers’ mark is on their faces from prostration, while they seek God’s bounty and pleasure. It makes the section’s sign, face, worship, and rıza images meet.
Criminals are known by their marks and seized on the Day scene. It supplies the adverse counterpart to the worshipper’s face-mark and the favorable face.
“We shall brand him on the snout” gives a literal punitive mark. It is a boundary for the section’s sign image: a mark can expose disgrace rather than identify the true Lord.

One dependent servant is a burden to his master wherever directed, while the other commands justice and is on a straight path. It makes servitude, direction, burden, and upright road a single parable.
A man owned by quarrelling partners is contrasted with one wholly belonging to one man, and the verse ends in praise. It clarifies why the section’s servant needs one true owner.
Joseph asks whether many separate lords are better or God, the One, the Overpowering. It turns the ownerless animal image into a question of whom one truly belongs to.
Joseph says judgment belongs only to God, who commanded worship of Him; that is the upright religion. Ownership, worship, and a right way cohere in his prison speech.
God contrasts a powerless owned slave with one freely given good provision who spends it. It makes the section’s owner, dependency, and bestowed provision concrete.
“Seek help through patience and prayer” is hard except for the humble. It supplies a Qur’anic form for the section’s worshipper who asks the owner for help.
Believers are told to seek help through patience and prayer, with God with the patient. It turns the requested aid of 1:5 into a sustained way of walking.
Moses tells his people to seek help from God and be patient, because the earth belongs to God. It joins help, endurance, and the true owner of the ground on which they walk.
“This is My straight path, so follow it; do not follow the ways” makes a single owned route stand against paths that scatter people from it.
The Prophet says his Lord has guided him to a straight path, an upright religion, the creed of Abraham. It connects the requested road to Abraham’s anti-idolatrous orientation.
God says obedience would guide them to a straight path. It makes the section’s prayed-for route an enacted response rather than a mere direction.
Those who obey God and the Messenger are with those God has favored. It identifies the “those You favored” of the section’s path by their companionship and obedience.
These are the prophets “whom God favored”; when the Merciful’s verses are recited, they fall prostrate and weep. Favor is shown as receptive, willing worship.
Those who hold fast to God receive mercy and bounty and are guided to Him by a straight path. It gives the road a destination in God Himself.
Those given knowledge recognize revelation as truth, believe, and their hearts humble; God guides believers to a straight path. This joins knowledge, submission, and route.
The Prophet is told that he guides to a straight path. It gives the section’s front-going guide a prophetic, not merely animal-herd, form.
Whoever holds fast to God has been guided to a straight path. The verse makes dependence on the true owner the grip that prevents straying.
“This is the path of your Lord, straight”; the signs are detailed for those who remember. It links path, Rabb, and recognisable signs as the section does.
Abraham is chosen and guided to a straight path after being grateful for God’s favors. It joins gratitude for نعمة to the Abrahamic road.
The Children of Adam are commanded not to worship Satan, their clear enemy. It gives the section’s voluntary worship a rival master from whom the road must turn.
Satan has led many of them astray. As the continuation of the worship/straight-path command, it gives the section’s stray ending its active misleader.
People who do not use heart, eyes, or ears are “like livestock—rather, more astray.” The herd image becomes a warning against human loss of the way.
Those who neither hear nor reason are likened to livestock, “rather more astray in way.” It directly reverses the section’s guided herd and leader.
The one who creates and proportioned supplies the section’s image of a Rabb who fits a creature for its course.
The one who determines and then guides puts measure and way together, reinforcing the section’s scale and guidance meeting.
The one who brings out pasture supplies the plant and herd provision that follows formation and guidance.
The green pasture becomes dark stubble. It provides a boundary within the section’s nourishing landscape: what is raised also passes.
